subtopic: MEDICAL CARE
MEDICAL CARE
subsubtopic: TWENTIETH ANNIVERSARY OF INTRODUCTION IN SASKATCHEWAN-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, 1 rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. Twenty years ago today, July 23, 1962, the Saskatoon Agreement was signed between the Saskatchewan NDP government represented by the late Premier W. C. Lloyd, by Bill Davies, then minister of health, by Allan Blakeney, chief negotiator, and the College of Physicians and Surgeons of Saskatchewan represented by Dr. H. Dalgleish. With this agreement the First universal prepaid compulsory medicare program came into existence in North America.
Today, as the principles of medicare are under attack from many directions, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin):
That this House dedicate itself in a new and firm resolution to protect this great social institution and pay tribute to Tommy Douglas, father of medicare, Lord Taylor, arbitrator of the dispute in 1962, and Bob Von Pilis who personally showed me and others the value of the long haul.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I, too, rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. In view of the fact that a new water-mill technology has been produced by a small firm in Dartmouth, Nova Scotia, called Nova Energy Limited, under contracts managed by the National Research Council, and whereas this technology, known as the vertical axis water turbine, eliminates the need for dams to produce hydroelectric power, and since the construction of dams has ruined entire river systems, caused the extermination of migratory fish species, changed the weather, and flooded good farm and forest lands, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Mission-Port Moody (Mr. Rose):
That this House express its unanimous support for the National Research Council and Nova Energy Limited in this environmental, economic and energy breakthrough, which could well make Canada a world leader in water-mill technology.

subtopic: SMALL BUSINESSES LOANS ACT (NO. 3) MEASURE TO AMEND

speakeroldname: Hon. Charles Lapointe (Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)) moved
speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
subtopic: SMALL BUSINESSES LOANS ACT (NO. 3) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
that Bill C-122, an act to amend the Small Businesses Loans Act (No. 3), be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.
He said: Madam Speaker, it is a privilege to start the debate on second reading of Bill C-122, whose purpose is to provide a nine-month extension for the Small Businesses Loans Act. Before going any further, I would like to mention that I had a number of conversations on the subject with my colleague, the member for Cambridge (Mr. Speyer) and also with my colleagues in the New Democratic Party, namely the member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) and the member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow). 1 know that the hon. member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn), who in the past has always shown an interest in small businesses, is also interested in this bill, as he indicated yesterday when he phoned my office to inquire about some details. My colleagues in the Progressive Conservative Party and the New Democratic Party informed me that they agreed with the principle and the purpose of the bill, which is to provide a nine-month extension for the Small Businesses Loans Act. I hope that today, and my colleagues realize this, we shall be able to dispose of all stages of this bill, namely, second reading, Committee of the Whole and third reading, because the act has ceased to exist since June 30 of this year. This means, Mr. Speaker, that the chartered banks and other financial institutions, which during the 21 years that the legislation has been in existence have been accustomed to making loans guaranteed 80 to 100 per cent by the Government of Canada, have agreed for the past weeks to continue operating under the provisions of the former act which expired on June 30, 1982. I personally wrote to the financial institutions and chartered banks, requesting them to extend their operations, mentioning that the government intended to extend
the act until the end of March 1983. If the banks and other financial institutions are to go on offering government guaranteed loans to small businesses, it is essential that this bill be passed, and I hope that with the collaboration of my colleagues in the Progressive Conservative Party and the New Democratic Party, we shall be able to pass this bill today.
Mr. Speaker, as the House is aware, the government has been regularly reviewing the Small Businesses Loans Act, either to provide a three-year extension or to change the maximum amount of loans admitted under the Small Businesses Loans Act. Hon. members will probably wonder, as did my colleague, the member for Mississauga South, yesterday, why only a nine-month extension? Why not three years, as usual? Mr. Speaker, there are two reasons for this. First of all, we want to administer the Small Businesses Loans Act according to the same schedule we use for the legislation on loans to fishermen and farmers. These two acts, Mr. Speaker, expire or run according to the Fiscal year, that is, from April 1 to March 31, and I would like the Small Businesses Loans Act to be administered according to the same calendar, instead of from January to December. My second reason is that, as the House is aware, about two months ago I made public a study on small business financing, which contains a chapter on the Small Businesses Loans Act. I am now setting up an advisory committee, consisting of Canadian businessmen and women, to analyse this study and make recommendations by the end of this year on any additional changes to be made in the Small Businesses Loans Act and in the government's general policy on the financing of small businesses.
That is why I am asking the House today to approve this nine-month extension. I am not now in a position to propose more substantial changes, since I first want to see the recommendations the advisory committee on small businesses will be making between now and the end of this year. Bill C-122 is very straightforward Mr. Speaker, and, in fact, it contains only one paragraph. However, it is a very important piece of legislation, because it amends an act that has far-reaching consequences. Since its first passage in 1961, the impact of the Small Businesses Loans Act has been very substantial and very favourable. In 21 years, nearly 100,000 loans totalling $2.7 billion were authorized under the act. When we realize, Mr. Speaker, that the maximum loan authorized is $100,000, a maximum that has been in effect for only two years, then we can imagine the vast number of businesses that have been assisted under this program.
The main characteristic of the program consists in helping small businesses obtain loans of up to $100,000, with the support of substantial government guarantees. If a business has a gross turnover of $1.5 million or less, it is eligible for
July 23, 1982

improvement or expansion loans with an 80 to 90 per cent guarantee by the Canadian government. For instance, the federal government will guarantee 80 per cent of the value of a loan that will be used to finance the purchase of fixed or movable equipment, including installation costs. If the loan is to be used for the purchase, renovation or construction of new premises or the purchase of land, this guarantee may be as high as 90 per cent and, of course, the loans must be paid back within ten years.
The interest rate applied to guaranteed loans under the Small Businesses Loans Act is also very competitive, which is why considerable use is made by small businesses of this mechanism. In fact, it is one of the attractive aspects of the act, since interest on the loans is 1 per cent above the prime rate, and unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, it is very often, if not always, the case that small businesses have trouble getting loans on such favourable terms. Very often, chartered banks or financial institutions charge 2 or 3 per cent above the prime rate on loans to small businesses. Since the act has been in existence for 21 years, I am sure my colleagues are aware of the basic components of the Small Businesses Loans Act, namely, who is eligible, on what terms, what the requirements are for the guarantee, and so forth. There are some aspects of this legislation, however, which I would like to recall for hon. members, because we tend to forget them too easily.
First of all I would like to mention that most Canadian businessmen and women-and I give them credit for it-in spite of the very strong government guarantees which, as I said before, over a period of 20 years have reached up to $2.7 billion, have dutifully met their loan commitments under this act. Requests for payment or request to the government to use the guarantee provided for these loans have represented only .8 per cent of total loans since the act was passed 21 years ago. In other words, the direct cost of application of the legislation has been extremely reasonable.
The second point that I would like to make concerning the Small Businesses Loans Act is that this legislation is a perfect example of government efficiency. Indeed, the administration of the act requires a staff of only six employees, including the support staff and the manager. If we consider, Mr. Speaker, that, last year, these six people approved and administered 12,500 loans totalling $502 million, I believe that it is easy to conclude that this represents a very substantial and efficient performance. My hon. friends on both sides of the House can play a major role by ensuring that this program, which is very popular among small businesses as well as being very important, receives as much publicity as possible. To assist them in this regard, and most Members of Parliament have already used this procedure, I am glad to make available to them and to send on request brochures and pamphlets that explain how to use the program, and I know that most members have made an effort to use this material to inform the business community in their constituencies about this program which gives them
Small Businesses Loans Act (No. 3)
relatively easy access to capital because of the government guarantee.
I would also like to say that it is important to pass this legislation immediately because, in addition to the 4 per cent reduction of interest rates announced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) in his budget of June 28, chartered banks, financial institutions, credit unions and Caisses populates will be able to use the loan guarantee mechanism up to an amount of $100,000 under the Small Businesses Loans Act on the loans they provide and to which the 4 per cent reduction in interest rates will apply. I therefore believe that a combination of these two programs will allow more businesses to go ahead with their plans to invest, modernize their businesses, purchase new equipment, and so on, and I am convinced that all of this will lead to the economic recovery which we all wish for.
I know that by giving approval to this bill, my colleagues will support a very popular piece of legislation which will extend the application of the act, and I can assure all hon. members that the small business sector will continue to make a wider use of this legislation and to benefit from its provisions. I therefore believe that today we have an opportunity, which happens perhaps too rarely in the House of Commons, for all parties to come to an agreement and legislate quickly and efficiently to assist the business community, which is truly the backbone of the Canadian economy. This is why I hope, Mr. Speaker, that the House will approve this bill quickly, and 1 would like to thank in advance my colleagues of the Progressive Conservative Party and the New Democratic Party for their co-operation in this regard.

anywhere near correct, since the first of the year. Indeed, it is nearly three times more than in previous years. speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
subtopic: SMALL BUSINESSES LOANS ACT (NO. 3) MEASURE TO AMEND

Mr. Speaker, the main reason for the wider use of the act is that prior to 1978 the recommendation in the act was that the interest rate to be applied by financial institutions should be of one below prime. There was not a great enthusiasm on the part of the financial community to apply this act because of that provision.
Following consultation with representative groups of small businesses and financial institutions in 1978, the decision was made to raise the interest rate to one above prime. Since then the financial institutions have been more aggressive in promoting this program. Looking at it in retrospect, considering the utilization of the act, the small business community has profited from it over the last few years.

subtopic: SMALL BUSINESSES LOANS ACT (NO. 3) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is the third amendment to the Small Businesses Loans Act in this session of Parliament. We started off with Bill C-17 which was cleaned up on June 6, 1980, followed by Bill C-84 which was cleaned up on December 16, 1981, and now we have Bill C-122 before us. Three times during this session of Parliament we have dealt with the Small Businesses Loans Act.
One begins to wonder what is wrong with a ministry which cannot get its act together. Why should the House of Commons in one session of Parliament have to deal with the Small Businesses Loans Act three times? Why could Parliament not do the job once and have it done and over with?
Bill C-122 implies that we must again deal with the Small Businesses Loans Act in this Parliament by March 31, 1983, less than eight months from now. The minister of small business is supposed to have everything in hand. It seems rather strange that he has to come to this House three times to explain that he wants to extend the act for.
The minister has given an explanation of that. Frankly, his explanation does not wash. The minister says it should be brought in line with the fiscal year end. That is no problem. He could have brought it in for the fiscal year end March 31, 1985, 1987 or whenever he wanted it. In other words, there is no problem getting it on a fiscal year end system.
The minister does not need to have the act expire at the end of this fiscal year. It could expire at the end of the fiscal year umpteen years from now. That argument is pretty shallow. The minister knows better than to produce such a shallow argument.
We come back to his concept of a blue ribbon committee. I do not know whether it will be called a little blue ribbon committee or what kind of blue ribbon committee it will be. It is another illustration by a government that refuses to trust Parliament. The minister knows that there are many members in this House who in their career prior to coming here were engaged in small business. A number of members are still
heavily involved in small business. While they are not fully employed in those businesses, they certainly have an interest in them.
Throughout the communities in each of our constituencies there are a great number of small businesses. If there is one matter that Members of Parliament know more about than anything else, it is small business, both personal and in their dealings with constituents. However, we have to recruit a paid, presumably, little blue ribbon committee to advise the minister. Therefore, we cannot extend this bill beyond March 31. After all, we have to wait for this committee to report.
I say to the minister that is a pretty shabby answer. If the minister really had wanted to get Parliament and the small business community on his side, he would have taken his financing report concerning small business and directed a reference to a special task force of this House to inquire into what the Government of Canada can do to expedite small business financing. Instead, we wind up with one little bill after another which is really an extension of the same bill with some little alteration. We wind up with a little blue ribbon committee rather than the opportunity to have Parliament get down to brass tacks and see what can be done with regard to small business financing.
There is really no excuse for this. The government has an obligation to use the resources of Parliament. Patronage-oriented committees to advise the minister so that he can stay far away from Members of Parliament and bring in to the House a fait accompli to be rubber-stamped is the wrong way to go.
If the minister wanted to reorganize small business financing, he could have arranged with his colleague the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Pinard) to direct the appointment of a special task force to inquire into proposals with respect to small business financing and make recommendations. There is expertise in this House in terms of small business financing. That was an opportunity for this minister to show that Parliament can be trusted.
As I pointed out to the minister in my questions before commencing my remarks, there has been a great use of the Small Businesses Loans Act, starting in 1978 and continuing on through. There has been an exponential growth in the use of this act by small business. One begins to wonder about that because in some senses this bill should not be called the Small Businesses Loans Act. It should be called the small business guarantee act for bankers, because that is what it does.
I noticed the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) smiling when he heard the explanation of the minister as to why the sudden explosion in the use of the Small Businesses Loans Act because of the fact the banks can now charge 1 per cent above prime and get a government guarantee. It is good to get 1 per cent over prime and still get government backing for a loan. That is a pretty good deal for a bank.
I think we should all be concerned about to what extent the Government of Canada will give the credit of the people of
July 23, 1982

Canada to a bank to allow it to charge 1 per cent above prime and somehow say that this is small businesses loans legislation and not what it really is, "bankers' guarantee legislation." In that sense these bills are really hokum because they claim to do something they really do not do at all. Loans are not being made by the government to small businesses in this situation. This is an arrangement whereby the Government of Canada is allowed to guarantee bank loans to small businesses up to $100,000. When we look at it in that sense, we begin to ask ourselves why the government did not trust Parliament and have a task force study the issue. There is really no answer to that. The government does not have its act together concerning small business at all.
The minister mentioned the provisions in the budget which provide for reducing interest rates on certain small business loans by 4 per cent, but that is not before the House. What I would like to be told by the minister or some government spokesman is why those budgetary provisions for relatively low interest abatement for small business are not before the house. This House is likely to adjourn, and some people say the House will not be reconstituted, perhaps, until some time approaching Thanksgiving. We have a promise in the budget respecting interest abatement or interest rebates for small business, but those rebates cannot be made until legislation is passed. Yet we are spending this afternoon debating a bankers' guarantee bill and not really doing anything for small business other than extending this guarantee bill. Why are we extending it only until March 31? The minister gave us a hokum explanation.
There has been very little lost under the Small Businesses Loans Act. Indeed, the lost ratio is less than the lost ratio the banks have suffered on their regular loan portfolios. One begins to wonder, then, why there is a government guarantee on those loans. Why do we need government guarantees when the loan loss performance is better than the regular loan loss performance of banks on regular, ordinary, every day loans in their general portfolios? I would have thought the minister or some representative of the government would be able to give us that rationale this afternoon. It is the kind of rationale a task force of this House would want. It is the kind of thing I would have thought would come from the minister. We have had an inquiry into bank profits. We are likely to be tabling a report in a very short time, and that report will indicate the loan losses by our chartered banks. The loan losses under this legislation are smaller than the regular loan losses determined by that committee.
The best thing we have ever had for small business was the proposal developed by my party under the leadership of the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) when he was minister of finance. He prepared and organized something called a Small Business Development Bond. Hon. members will recall that the government accepted the idea in April of 1980. It fooled around with the idea. It said it would never allow it to be implemented. We on this side of the House conducted a bit of a filibuster and forced the minister finally to
Small Businesses Loans Act (No. 3)
get some clout in cabinet and to have that Small Business Development Bond program instituted. It ran until December 31, 1981. During the period under that proposal small businesses were able to borrow money at roughly half prime plus 2 per cent. The cash flow costs of loans under that program were 9 per cent or 10 per cent. Small businesses in the country borrowed capital funds amounting to over $2 billion over a nine-month period.
That program worked well. It was a dramatic help to small business. Unfortunately, that program went by the boards. The government's program of 4 per cent interest abatement is just so much air because the government has not enough intestinal honesty or fairness to introduce a bill which indicates where that type of program is going. Nothing will happen. No banks will make any loans. No banks made any loans under the Small Business Development Bond until we as a party on this side of the House forced the matter into the Income Tax Act in specific detail. No bank will lend under the government's 4 per cent-off interest proposal until the details of the proposal are forced into law in an accurate way so that they can be understood.
There seems to be a pattern with this government with respect to small business. The government produces a bill and says, "Yes, we passed another bill for small business, the Small Businesses Loans Act extension; aren't we wonderful fellows?" The minister can put out press releases on this every six, eight, nine or ten months and he can put out press releases on measures taken in the budget, but he has never done anything. This bill is nothing new and really does nothing. It is hokum. We are prepared to let it go through this afternoon, but at the same time we expect some explanation from the government. We expect an explanation from the minister as to where we are going better than the explanation he has given us so far.

subtopic: SMALL BUSINESSES LOANS ACT (NO. 3) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 want to thank my colleague the hon. member for Burlington (Mr. Kempling) for allowing me this opportunity to speak. I have a commitment that requires me to leave. 1 will be back, of course, but 1 wanted to say a word or two on this bill on behalf of my colleagues. 1 do not intend to take too long.
The hon. member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) went into the detail of a number of different pieces of legislation that may in one way or another assist small business. Without any disrespect for what he was saying, I thought that in terms of the over-all programs of the government as they apply to small business, we tend to deal with things in a very piecemeal fashion. There are numerous temporary measures available but these do not instil confidence and are not as well used, in normal circumstances, as they should be. They do not provide the service and the benefit that they are intended to provide. This is mainly because the people who take advantage of the reduced interest rates available through the Small Businesses Loans Act or the financial institutions that make the money available are never absolutely sure whether the legislation will be changed or terminated. It is therefore a little difficult for the lender or borrower to take advantage of the legislation in planning the expansion of business.
Someone may think that they would like to expand their business but are not yet to ready to proceed because there is still planning to be done, such as analyses of markets, a review of available machinery, possible change of location and the time it takes to formulate and execute an over-all plan. All of this may take longer than is allowed by the termination date in the bill. They are therefore unable to do much financial planning although that may well be the key element of any
expansion. They may decide that business opportunities justify an increase in capacity but they are not yet sure how to make the changes and whether in the short run that increase would be sufficient to pay the cost of the borrowing. If their calculations are made on the basis of the money available under the Small Businesses Loans Act, that means they must go ahead with their plans before the end of March next year. In some cases they may not be able to do this.
I wonder why the minister did not simply extend the bill without a termination date. I heard his explanation that a committee was being set up, but that committee need not interfere with the termination date. The bill could have been extended for an indeterminate period of time. People could then plan and it would give some stability to their planning to know that the money is likely to be available if, as and when they are ready to take advantage of it. This would be of more benefit to them and perhaps the legislation would then be used more widely.
I am always concerned that we may expect people to rush into things. With the present termination date the small business person may feel it necessary to make decisions more quickly than his business justifies. The sensible decision may well be not to expand, if they are not sure that the moneys will be available. That kind of decision will cost us job opportunities and economic development.
I suggest to the minister that he give serious thought to going ahead with the committee to study the problems of small business-although I think these are self-evident-and that he extend the terms of the act without including a termination date. This would allow the business community to feel secure in the knowledge that it would be able to avail itself of the capital that is required when it has had an opportunity to review plans.
We support the change, Mr. Speaker. We hope that it will provide benefits. There would have been no benefit if we had not provided for an extension because the bill had already run out.
1 have a varied background, Mr. Speaker, and over the years 1 have owned two small businesses, either in partnership or outright. Both of them made money. I sold one and gave one away. The problem that very small businesses have at the moment is not that of expansion but of being able to use their productive capacity. The bill will not help in that regard.
The problem with the majority of small businesses is that they are unable to find a market for their product. There is an ever diminishing marketplace for a number of reasons, partly because of the general economic downturn which has resulted in fairly substantial numbers of people becoming unemployed, and partly because of very high interest rates at the consumer level, which range upwards of 22 per cent. If someone is buying on credit they may pay as much as 27 or 28 per cent interest. The difficulty facing the small business person is that the consumer marketplace is small. The cost of the product manufactured or sold increases, the cost of carrying the inventory is going up as a result of interest rates, and the
July 23, 1982

number of people available to purchase the product is going down. Fewer people feel confident enough to spend the money that they have or to assume the additional liability of a major purchase.
I suggest to the minister that, notwithstanding the best intentions on the bill or the fact that I think it has general support in the House, it does not really begin to address the major problems of small business. I am sure that in the ridings of every member of this House-I know it is true in those of the New Democratic Party-every day there are announcements of businesses that are going bankrupt or simply closing their doors, and this does not help. Other than in a few isolated instances it is very difficult to find a great deal of initiative being shown by people in the small business sector towards expansion of their business. After all, who is going to expand their business if their customers are not in a position to buy? I suggest to the minister responsible for small business that he devote not only time to finding ways to help those who require financial assistance to expand, but that he put some conscious effort into finding ways to stimulate the consumer marketplace.
Look at what has happened to the country since we last dealt with this bill. The level of unemployment has gone from 800,000 or 900,000 to in excess of 1.5 million, almost double. Of course, that has impacted most heavily on the small business community. Tens of thousands of people are not eligible for unemployment insurance because they have been unemployed for longer than the act will allow payment to be made. They have had an income reduction so dramatic that they are unable to make purchases, and that impacts primarily on the small business community. To turn a blind eye to that problem is to turn a blind eye to the most serious of all of the problems confronting small business.
I am dismayed when I look at the government's over-all strategy-it is no secret that I disagree with the strategy- because the government has determined, for whatever reason, that it is appropriate to reduce the purchasing power of Canadians even further and restrict their incomes even more. If a person's wage level today is such that he is unable to purchase the things being manufactured, and therefore more and more people are laid off and more and more small businesses are unable to continue in operation, if that is the situation today-and I think it is without question-how will restricting their incomes even further improve things? If you restrict their incomes by legislation or otherwise so that they will have less, how will that improve the situation?
I say to you, Mr. Speaker, and through you to the minister, that I really do think we in this House are dealing more with the symptoms that we are with the results. We are not dealing with the major issue, but we will support the bill because if it can be of some assistance then, of course, we should. But we in this House have to find a way to deal with the real problems of small business.
Small Businesses Loans Act (No. 3)
I say, Mr. Speaker, that the real problems are directly the result of the government's over-all economic policy. It is not a matter of whether or not we should have a Small Businesses Loans Act or a small business development bond. We should have those things, but by themselves they are cosmetic. We must confront the fundamental problem and we will not do that by going home for the summer, much though I think everyone here deserves to do that. But we will not be able to confront the problem by being away until October. I am not preaching for another session, believe me, but I am saying that when I look at this legislation and consider the impact it will have, and when I look at the over-all government economic policy and I consider that it will in itself destroy much of what this is intended to help solve, then I have to think the government is wrongheaded and does not understand. Or, if it does understand, then for some reason which escapes me it has chosen to disregard the current economic difficulties of this country which are-well, I was going to say almost the government's sole responsibility, but I think that is unfair. Certainly there is an impact from what happens outside the country, but the problems are such that, at least in part, it is within the ability of the government to find a solution.
The government has a number of options open to it which could help stimulate the consumer end of the marketplace. By so doing it would make it possible for small business people to generate the revenue necessary to continue to provide the goods and services they can and should be providing.
So while it is clear we support this bill, we do so only because it is one of a number of measures which may be of some marginal assistance. But the over-all problem cannot be solved in this piecemeal way, with a cosmetic effort. The overall problem rests squarely in the lap of the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen), and I suggest to the minister responsible for small business that it is to the Minister of Finance that he must make his earnest plea. This country and its businesses cannot survive unless we are prepared to change the economic direction the country is taking.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subtopic: SMALL BUSINESSES LOANS ACT (NO. 3) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to say a few words on Bill C-122 which will amend the Small Businesses Loans Act. It does so by extending the termination date for loans to be guaranteed from June 30, 1982 to March 31, 1983. The fact that this bill was brought in today, July 23, approximately 23 days after the guarantee of the government for loans has expired, is an indication, at least to me, that the government really does not have too much concern for the small business community. I say that with no reflection on the minister. I believe the minister is an honest person and that he tries to do the very best he can for the small business community under the conditions under which he has to labour.
Let me return to comments made by some other members regarding the rate that small-business men have to pay for the loans they get under the Small Businesses Loans Act. Initially the rate was set by statute. The rate set was below the lowest rate which the banks had for their best accounts. Consequently, hardly anyone could get a loan under the Small Businesses Loans Act. In fact, the whole thing used to be quite a joke. We used to ask the minister of finance, who was John Turner at the time, "What are we going to do about the Small Businesses Loans Act?" Small businessmen used to go into their banks only to be told that they, the banks, had never heard of the Small Businesses Loans Act. If they were not told that, the bank officials would say that they had to get a hold of head office because they did not know anything about the act at the branch.
The minister of finance would tell us that he was having lunch with the chairman of the Canadian Bankers' Association and that he would mention the problem. I can just imagine the difficulty of small business people getting loans under the Small Businesses Loans Act being discussed between the shrimp cocktail and the double martini. That was just a lot of nonsense. We would ask the minister again and we would hear him ask for the name of the bank and the branch and that he would look into it. At that point we began to flood him with names of branches that were befuddling their customers.
Finally, the criteria for establishing the interest rate were changed and the act was amended. It was decided to take a selection of government bonds and to have the rate equal to the average yield of those bonds. It was rather a complicated formula, but the bottom fell out of the bond market and the rate was lower than ever. The banks complained that it was their money that was being lent and there was no way they would be lending at 1 per cent or 2 per cent below what they gave to their best accounts. The situation fuddled-duddled on for a number of years. Finally, the act was amended and we saw a sudden upsurge of loans under the Small Businesses Loans Act in 1978. That is just a little of the background to the Small Businesses Loans Act, but that game playing has gone on for at least ten or 12 years. In those days the only people who got a loan under the Small Businesses Loans Act were the best customers of the bank.
I recall visiting with a small retailer who was well financed, long established and did not need money under the Small Businesses Loans Act. He told me that he had just got a loan under the act. He was very happy, but he was surprised to get it. At the time bank managers were giving out these loans as a kind of prize. The minister of finance had leaned on the banks and they decided they would give out a certain percentage of loans across the country, which goes to show a lot of game playing was going on.
I want to address myself to some other aspects of the Small Businesses Loans Act and perhaps I can make some suggestions to the minister. It is in the small business community that the beginnings of a recovery in our economy will take place. If our economy is going to recover, that is where it will start. Recovery does not commence with megaprojects. I was really astounded to hear the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray) say that the government was looking into a $500 million investment in Airbus with some European manufacturers. The recovery will begin with the small business sector of the country.
It is stability of the economy that we require. If we look at it broadly, we will see that usually when the economy turns down most small-business men retain their staff because the most important thing they have is people. Of all the products they have, people are the most important. They have to compete with large enterprises for people. In order to keep their enterprises going they retain people, whether the economy goes up or down. This imparts tremendous stability on the economy of the country.
The government must recognize that there is no shortage of entrepreneurship, innovative ability or inventiveness in the country, but there is a shortage of venture capital to get things going. The Small Businesses Loans Act is too restrictive in terms of capital expenditures.
I have spoken on this matter many times before. I have suggested to the government that at least the Small Businesses Loans Act could be expanded. On March 31, or hopefully before that date, when this matter comes up again, I hope we can broaden it somewhat. For instance, I would like to see the act expanded to allow small-business men to purchase technology or patents which are already in operation. There is a lot of patent technology available for small-business men to purchase and produce in this country. Also I would like to see it arranged that a small business loan could be acquired for the registering of a patent. It is most important that some means or mechanism be found to allow them to do this.
The minister said that he was setting up a committee to study the financing of small businesses. He does not have to do that because there are enough people, as the hon. member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) said in this Parliament, such as John Bulloch's progressive organization, the Canadian Federation of Independent Business and other small business organizations in the country, who have studied the matter to
July 23, 1982

death. They know how to finance small business; they know what is required.
The difficulty is that the only place where small-business men can go for any kind of term financing today is the banks. They used to be able to go to professional people who had funds available to invest, but that was before the days of the capital gains tax. Now that we have a capital gains tax some of the funds are siphoned off. Today, with the government paying 19.5 per cent on Canada Savings Bonds and such, what is the percentage in taking a flyer on a small business venture or new idea? Investors can put their money into Canada Savings Bonds at 19.5 per cent. There is no risk; they can just sit back and clip coupons. Why take a chance unless there is opportunity for unusual gain?
We must find a mechanism to get money into the small business sector. We should allow innovative individuals and inventors to use the Small Businesses Loans Act to finance some of their research and development, to acquire a patent which is already in place, or to register a patent on their inventions.
Let us take a look at what is imported into the country. It is absolutely amazing. We do not have to start a buy-Canada project or to wave the flag. We should just make facilities available through adjustments in taxation, and we will be amazed at what will happen. Today the Canadian dollar is selling at quite a discount. It is a disaster to some people who are importing; it is an advantage to some people who are exporting. But there is a strategy which can be used. There are various products shipped into the country which can be had on a licensing arrangement. The easiest thing in the world is to go to someone with a product who wants to ship it into Canada. When he looks at the tariffs, the freight rates, the discount on the Canadian dollar and the laid down cost of the product in our market, he suddenly realizes that there will not be a very great sale for the product, but he wants to move into the market perhaps to take advantage of some of the worldwide advertising which would be involved.
I know this method works because I have done it myself. We should go to companies and say that we would like to make their products available in Canada under licence. We could give them the reasons and show them the numbers. But we are not doing this because the required venture capital is just not available.
I am suspicious of committees. The minister floated out the idea that the committee would be studying the financing of small businesses, their problems and so forth. 1 will be very surprised if anything comes of it. 1 think it is just a typical bureaucratic manoeuvre-here is a problem, everyone is pressing on it, let us put it out to a study group. We will never hear about it again. If we hear something positive from it, I will be the first one to congratulate the minister publicly. I can almost wager that nothing will really happen; it will just be another report.

speechtext:
Just a moment. I will not say that he was dishonest, but I will say that perhaps the thrust of the government of the day was as the minister stated and it was not the intention to make it compulsory. I think that was an honest statement. He went out and said that in all honesty, but down the line the entire game plan changed. Thus, my comments on metric were made in that atmosphere. I do not deny them; I said them. They are on the record. But I have never seen such dishonesty in the representation of those comments as I have seen in some of the letters to the editor which have been quoted broadly across the country. I realize they are using me as a sucker,
Having said that, I want to return to the subject or else you will call me back to it, Mr. Speaker. In 1979 I believe we had the beginnings of a solution to the problems of financing small businesses through the Small Business Development Bond. 1 would hope that the minister would look into that device again and urge the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) to introduce something similar to it once again. This is necessary because we need a source of investment capital beyond the banks. It makes no sense simply to tell small-business men to go to the bank and pay their rates. They need another source of funds either through a Small Business Development Bond or some other instrument, as has been suggested by many small business people, so that they can acquire funds through various sources where the interest on those funds is tax free. Small businesses need a device for obtaining funds at a lower rate than is available at banks.
The money is available. It is common knowledge that there is more money on deposit in the chartered banks of this country on a per capita basis than in any other country in the

July 23, 1982
Small Businesses Loans Act (No. 3)
western world. Canadians are very good at saving their money. In times of high inflation as exists today, people are squirreling money away in large amounts. We must find a mechanism to encourage people to withdraw their savings so they can be put to use to employ people and develop services which are so vitally needed in this country.
This country will survive despite our present economic conditions and despite the mismanagement of the government opposite. Our country is too strong to fail. We still have talented people although they have been somewhat disheartened by the conditions we are in. There is no shortage, however, of people with novel ideas and those who are adventurous. I am dismayed, though, at the number of people who say that they would give up on Canada and move to the United States. I urge them to stay and fight the battle because I believe our future is unparalleled.
The engine for the recovery of the economy of Canada is the small business sector. I have talked to small business entrepreneurs and they do not want the government in their pockets or on their backs. They do not want a large bureaucracy which requires the completion of so many forms. I have told the story many times of when I sat in my business office, where I had two large stacks of paper on my desk. One stack consisted of a pile of forms from Statistics Canada. I had to decide whether I would work on that pile or go through the other papers which could possibly yield a profit on which I would pay a tax. I had to make a decision since the pile of paper from Statistics Canada was growing. Since I am a very practical person I went to the local stationery store and ordered a rubber stamp which said "Not Applicable". With the red stamp pad which I purchased I stamped the words "Not Applicable" on that stack of Statistics Canada forms. I opened a file and put my copies in it and sent the originals back to Statistics Canada without even putting a stamp on the envelope.
In due course I received a computerized letter from Statistics Canada which said "We are in receipt of form No."- whatever the number was-"which we understand is"-and they had written in the word "Not Applicable". It was signed with a scribbled signature. We simply put that letter in the file. When the next form came in I again stamped it "Not Applicable" and returned a copy of the letter. Through this process we managed to cut down our Statistics Canada paper over a 14-month period.
I am not suggesting that this is the solution to the problem. I merely give that as an example of what happened and still occurs today. If the minister wishes to form a committee to look for practical solutions, I would suggest that he set up a committee comprised of someone from the Department of National Revenue, an official from Statistics Canada, someone from the Department of Finance as well as representatives from some large accounting firms so that they can devise a simplified accounting system for the small retailer and small-business man. This system would easily allow the small entrepreneur to make use of the statistics that he desires and when he makes his annual return he can supply a form which has the statistics that Statistics Canada require. This would be
a step in the right direction and would help small entrepreneurs in the operation of their businesses.
In 1979 my colleague for Capilano (Mr. Huntington) was the minister of state for small business. I will not cast judgment on the present Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism (Mr. Lapointe) yet since he has some time to go in his job. As I say, I believe he is honest and trying to do a good job in difficult circumstances. The hon. member for Capilano who was the minister in 1979 had a clear understanding of the concept of how to run the small business ministry. I was most heartened to see his approach to small business and encouraged by his receptiveness and understanding of the ideas received from the small business community. In the short time he was in office he set it on a good, straight course.
When the hon. member for Capilano took office he found the affairs of that ministry appalling. The government had been masquerading under the title of small business ministry because it consisted of a minister, a speech writer, a public relations person, a couple of researchers and a secretary. That was the extent of the small business ministry. Obviously, when we would ask questions we would get "nothing" answers from the minister because his department was just window dressing with little substance.
In summary, there is no shortage of entrepreneurs and inventors and innovative people with ideas in this country. However, I am sorry to say that many of them are leaving to go to the United States. I have interviewed a number of these people during the years I have been in Parliament and have listened to the difficulties they have had in trying to obtain money.
For example, I spoke to an entrepreneur in 1978. He came to my office to tell me that he had a very fine mechanical elevating device used in building maintenance. He could not seem to convince anyone in the banking system to advance money to him to begin his venture, so he decided to take his model to a trade show in the United States. He found many interested people there and signed four of them as distributors while taking an order for about 15 of these devices. He returned to his local banker and said, "I have these orders. They are worth a few hundred thousand dollars". The banker said, "They are no good to us as collateral until they are accounts receivable". He would not give him any bridge financing or any funds to build the devices.
This entrepreneur then went back to his distributors in the United States to tell them what happened. Those distributors said, "Come to New York state, we will arrange to have a plant built for you". Therefore, he took this device from Canada to the United States. It is now being produced in the United States and is imported into Canada. This story happens time and time again. I am not blaming the government but I am saying that the engine is there, the ingenuity is there, the businesses are there and the ideas are there. There must be some mechanism to finance those businesses so they can begin to produce and hire people to develop and sell products.
July 23, 1982

I want to say a final word on research and development because I myself have engaged in a number of R and D projects over the years. What turns off research and development projects is not the lack of ideas, as there are many kinds of ideas, not the lack of engineering ability or anything of that type, but the lack of cash. One day one's comptroller or accountant says, "We have to pay bills and we have a payroll to meet. Now we will have to make a decision. Either you stop that gimmick that you are developing and let us use the money to pay our bills and our payroll, or we cannot continue." That is what really happens. If one knows where to look, one can see all sorts of partially completed ideas which are very good and would have a market, but they are stalled for lack of cash.
1 have put this idea forward on a number of occasions and I will state it briefly again. We should allow the small business community, those who have the capacity in the field of manufacturing, to undertake research and development projects and allow them to accumulate funds which they can deduct from their tax payment. We can devise the mechanisms for it, but that money should be specifically set aside for research and development projects. When there is sufficient money, they should be able to draw on that money, just as one can with a registered retirement savings plan. There should be the same concept for research and development. If one has a pretty good idea as to what it will cost to develop somehing, one should be able to draw down the money and get the project under way, knowing that one has the cash to complete it. One should not be able to use that cash for anything other than that research and development project. There should be a linkage mechanism with the Small Businesses Loans Act so that one if one finds oneself in the position where the project is almost complete but a little more money is needed to complete it, one can complete that project and get it out into the marketplace.
That is the sort of thing which must be done and a whole bunch of government grants would not be necessary. All that is needed is to put an administrative mechanism into place to allow that to happen. Whether or not the government holds the R and D money is really beside the point; the administrative details can be worked out. But I tell hon. members that we must have some means whereby the cash is available to complete these projects; otherwise the promoters will leave Canada and go to the United States, Great Britain and to other countries. We will lose those projects and end up importing many of those great ideas back into the country.
I have spoken for about 30 minutes of the time allotted to me in this debate. I know we have agreed to pass this bill in all stages and that there are other hon. members in the House who wish to make a contribution. Therefore, I thank Your Honour for your kind attention to some of the thoughts I have put forward in a positive and not critical sense. 1 hope some of them have been considered and that they will be explored a little further. Like all my colleagues, I am always available to discuss them in more detail with the minister or members of his staff at any time.

Mr. Speaker, if we listen to the official opposition, there seems to be no end of problems in this country. I would like to say a few words about the need for amending the Small Businesses Loans Act, since Bill C-122, an act to amend the Small Businesses Loans Act, is extremely important at this time. First, 1 should like to say a few words on our past experience, which has in fact been quite good for small businesses, and on the financing situation, to which the member for Burlington (Mr. Kempling) was referring earlier when he said that there was a considerable problem in getting lenders to offer loans to small businesses. Well, Mr. Speaker, in 1981, although there were problems, it seems the number of lenders other than chartered banks rose from 762 to 1,286. I do not know whether that could qualify as a problem, but I think there has been a good deal of progress in this area, and since the government is guaranteeing these loans, I believe that lending institutions other than banks will become more and more numerous. I should also like to say a few words about the act's historical background, the amendments made since 1961 regarding eligibility and reasons for application, and certain results which came to light during the last financial year and which were very encouraging.
The Small Businesses Loans Act came into effect in January, 1961, and its initial purpose was to encourage private lenders to provide fixed-term loans for small businesses. The act, which provides the lender with a guarantee against all losses, was initially to be effective for three years and was subsequently renewed at regular intervals. The act now in effect actually expired on June 30 of this year, and as the minister pointed out this morning, the act was to be extended for nine months so that it would expire at the same time as the legislation on loans to farmers and fishermen.
Since 1961, many amendments have been made to the act, and I shall name a few of the more important ones. In 1974, the maximum amount of loans repayable by any borrower was raised from $25,000 to $50,000 to allow for the expansion of the small business sector, an increasingly encouraging factor which required broader credit margins. In 1977, the maximum permissible loan from any lender was raised to $75,000 and the business turnover figure was raised to $1,500,000. In January, 1978, the interest rate formula was amended to allow lenders to charge prime plus 1 per cent. In 1978, responsibility for administering the act was transferred from the Department of Finance to the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce. In 1980, the amount of the loan offered by any lender was raised from $75,000 to $100,000. Mr. Speaker, further changes are expected, since an advisory committee has been formed to review all aspects of this legislation.
Under this legislation all Canadian chartered banks are deemed to be lending institutions. As a result of the amendments made in March, 1970, the scope of the act was enlarged

July 23, 1982
Small Businesses Loans Act (No. 3)
to include credit unions, Caisses populaires, trust companies, insurance companies and finance companies which are eligible and apply for designation by the minister. There have been many changes and those who were eligible were people in manufacturing, wholesale trade, retail trade, service businesses, communications, construction and other fields.
Naturally, there have been changes as well in the reasons why people submit applications, and loans may now be approved for purchasing real estate or movables, improving or modernizing facilities or premises, buying or building accommodation and even acquiring land. This has been a net improvement because the act has evolved with time and, as other members pointed out earlier, it will continue to evolve and to adjust to the needs of the very important small business sector. Particularly in Quebec, people are aware that small businesses play an extremely active role in our economic development and that they create hundreds of jobs. Mr. Speaker, during that short time period, under the Small Business Loans Act, 99,500 loans have been granted so far, for a total value of roughly $2 billion. In 1981 alone, 16,942 loans were approved for a total of $501,000. I have other figures which concern Quebec more particularly.
In 1981, 5,431 loans were approved as compared with 5,188 in 1980, an increase of 4.7 per cent. Even more encouraging is the fact that those loans amounted to $124 million in 1980 and about $147 million in 1981, up 18.8 per cent. This upward trend can be explained by the fact that many more lenders invaded the market to provide assistance to small businesses, particularly since the loans were fully guaranteed by the government, and I think that additional funds will be available for small businesses. As was stated before, I think that the extension of this act and the possibility of amending it further in the future deserve special consideration, particularly in 1982. Like all hon. members, I would be pleased if Bill C-122 were to be adopted as soon as possible so that it can benefit small businesses throughout Canada.

When you get into debt financing at interest rates that small business has had to endure recently, it does not allow small business to expand or to be created. If a person with some savings could get a 20 per cent return by investing in a small business, that would be all right. However, why risk putting money into a small business when you can get 20 per cent from the federal government?
We must address the matter of equity financing. The former parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance, the hon. member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans), and I have had discussions in the past on equity financing. We both agree that there has to be equity financing. However, we have a different viewpoint as to how it should be approached. He had a good suggestion, that of bringing the FBDB into equity financing. I object to that because I am worried that it will create a new bureaucracy. Small business does not need any more red tape. However, it may be a beginning.
He suggested that it could be like the CDC where there is private as well as government participation. When it reaches a certain point, you could sell that small business development corporation and it would become a public vehicle held by a number of small investors.
We both acknowledge that we come from a different philosophical base. I would rather see this done with incentives through our tax system. I would like to see some of the incentives that were in the tax system put back in. The small-business man cannot do it with debt financing alone. The average person does not have enough money to set up a business that will sustain itself without outside financing. Where the small-business man really needs help is during the early days of formation when cash flows are not adequate to

The minister mentioned today that these loans are principally for expansion, extension of a plant or new plant equipment.
I understand why the loan is so small. Not many people are thinking of expansion; they are looking for survival. Today in small business it is a question of survival. An industry cannot be expanded if it is laying off employees and its sales are down. Our problem is that we have not provided proper incentives to people to start industries. According to federal estimates, our national debt will reach some $122.7 billion this fiscal year. The cost of servicing this will consume 22 per cent of all federal spending.

The National Energy Program and the Foreign Investment Review Agency have sent out clear signals to all foreign investment that it is not welcome in Canada. All we have to do is look at the cash flow difficulties we have experienced. Traditionally, on a yearly basis, we have had a cash outflow of $2 billion, but last year the outflow was in excess of $10 billion. Corporate bankruptcies have increased from under 4,000 in 1977 to a current annual rate of 12,000.
As the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Fennell) said, the largest small business sector in the country is probably the farming sector. These recommendations are the first step forwards assuring Canadians long-term economic development, and I would like to share them with the House today.

We indicated we should withdraw totally the November 12 budget and replace it with an economic plan which would promote job creation and development through private investment. That is exactly the opposite of what this government has done. We indicated that we should get moving on major national projects to stimulate the economy, create jobs and meet urgent national and regional needs. These recommendations, Mr. Speaker, deliberately did not provide detailed plans or remedies for our economic salvation. Before we can devise specific policies and programs there must be fundamental changes in attitudes and psychology. Cooperatively, we must work together as a government and individuals to discover and implement economic solutions. We would also recognize and create an entrepreneurial culture which would permit our economic strategies to work. We must restore public trust and economic confidence. Without them we will not be able to unleash the initiative of the Canadian people themselves which is needed, as one expert who appeared before the committee put it, "to reintroduce market forces and profitability". When we were in government for that very short period of time, Mr. Speaker, we changed more than the faces of government. We changed the economic philosophy, spirit and direction of the government. This philosophy was borne out by our intention to create new wealth through the private sector and through a series of measures to reduce the deficit and build on provincial and regional strength, rather than fighting with our provincial colleagues. We wanted to develop measures to develop human resources. We adopted a six-point national economic development strategy to provide a structure and foundation for the government's support of economic advancement. Measures undertaken within the perimeters of each of these points serve to highlight the differences between what we stood for as a government and what the governing party, the Liberals, stand for.
Rather than go into any detail I just wish to mention the six areas so that they are on record. We had started to take steps in this area during the period of time we were in government, and it is interesting to note that even though we were in reality reducing government spending and the deficit, the Social Policy Planning Board of Canada indicated that our budget was the most socially progressive budget introduced in Canada in the past ten years. We were simply eliminating a great deal of government mismanagement. In addition to that, we were helping those who required help from their federal government. I am more than happy to go into specifics but I know there are a number of members who wish to participate in this debate, so I will just say that our policies reflected our deep belief in the worth of individual Canadians and their ability to develop themselves and also to develop a sound economic policy.
We in Canada enjoy many benefits, more than any other nation in the world. We have an abundance of natural resources, and on a much greater scale we have a great potential for human development, and we in this party wish to see that development occur. Even though I wish we could have served a great deal longer in government, I am thankful we had that period of time so that we could draw a comparison between what we did in government and what is being done now. All we have to do is to look at the record of the present administration to find that they have given us record government spending, record budget deficits, record high unemployment, taxation, inflation and interest rates, and that our dollar has reached a record low level. 1 ask members opposite: what are you doing to help the pensioner other than limiting the indexation of their pensions? In reality, you are going to reduce the income of those individuals who built this country, and some help that is. I ask the minister responsible for small business what policies he has advocated since he has had this portfolio other than gutting the Small Business Development Bond? We in this House, Mr. Speaker, so often find ourselves philosophically at opposite ends. I would like to share with the House my reasons for believing strongly in the individual initiative of Canadians, the so-called free-enterprise system. It cannot be denied that public opinion has been moulded into an anti-capitalist mentality. John Galbraith, who in my opinion is living proof that economics is an inexact science, has written a book called "Economics and the Public Purpose". He has researched the market arrangements of our economy and says it has given us inadequate housing, a terrible mass transit, poor health care and a host of other miseries. For the first time, to my knowledge, Mr. Galbraith comes out from behind the white cloak of liberalism and openly proclaims that the only answer to our problem is socialism.
Well, he deals in fairy tales, as do our Liberal friends opposite. This system of ours, the so-called free-enterprise system, is gradually shifting to a socialistic state under the leadership of our present Prime Minister. In the 1900s a majority of people lived below what we consider to be the poverty line; two thirds of them lived in substandard housing. Today, Mr. Speaker, the figure is less than 10 per cent. Ninety-five per cent of the people in Canada today have a daily minimum intake of nutrients essential to maintain health. Ninety-nine per cent of Canadian homes have gas or electric kitchen appliances. Ninety-six per cent of homes have TV sets. There are thousands of automobiles and trucks owned by our people, all of them on your street every day when you are in a hurry. Some people will point out that this is evidence of our materialism, but we have been the most generous of people. We have shared our wealth widely among our people, and we support with voluntary contributions various churches, libraries, symphonies, operas and non-private theatres.
If Mr. Galbraith is right, Mr. Speaker, and socialism is the answer, we do not have to theorize about it because we have a concrete example that we can look to for comparison. We can be just like that very great nation, Russia, rich in natural resources, with 250 million capable people and 60 uninterrupted years of socialism. As I say, we could be just like them; all it would require is a little bit of doing. To be like them we would have to cut our pay cheques by 75 per cent, move thousands of workers back to the farms, abandon two thirds of our steelmaking capacity, destroy thousands of TV sets, tear up miles of highway and railroad tracks, junk 19 out of 20 automobiles, knock down 70 per cent of our houses, and rip out 90 per cent of our telephones. Then all we would have to do is to find a capitalist country to sell us wheat on credit so that we would not starve.
That is why I believe in our free-enterprise system and that is why I think we who have the opportunity to serve in Parliament have to offer incentives rather than handouts to our small business sector.
Unless this government opposite comes to grips with the sad state of the economy which is affecting not only our small business sector but our pensioners and home owners, the rage which is evident in Canada is going to break out. As I indicated earlier in my remarks, that rage is going to explode. Quite frankly, it is evident when one enters the Parliament Buildings on a daily basis that the security people in the House of Commons are concerned about the explosion of that rage. One only has to see the Prime Minister entering and the increased number of security staff around him. I would hope that individuals like the Minister of Transport and the minister responsible for small business would react positively to the deep concerns evident right now throughout the population of Canada.

subtopic: SMALL BUSINESSES LOANS ACT (NO. 3) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-122, an act to amend the Small Businesses Loans Act, really does not address the problems facing small business across Canada. All
July 23, 1982

we are really doing is extending from July 1, 1980, to March 31, 1983, the Small Businesses Loans Act. Instead of bringing legislation forward in this way we should be bringing it in to assist small-business men in a genuine way. The problems facing small business today are due to government economic mismanagement, and it is forcing many businesses and farms into bankruptcy.
I think all members know full well that a farm operation is a small business in the truest sense of the word. In 1981 a record 8,055 businesses were forced to close their doors forever. Business bankruptcies in 1981 were 22 per cent higher than in 1980, and 43 per cent higher than in 1979. That should tell everyone in this House that there is something serious going on in the business community across Canada.
We all know, Mr. Speaker, that the individual businessman, the small entrepreneur, the little storekeeper, the barber shop and so on, provide fully 55 per cent of all employment across the country. We become alarmed when General Motors, a very large corporation, has to lay off people. We become alarmed when a mining operation in the northern part of Canada closes down and lays off people. I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that the underpinning of our whole economic system is the small-business man and the farmer. Yet we can read the statistics supplied by StatsCan into the record time and time again and very little alarm is expressed. What kind of things do we hear? Well, there is a downturn in the economy. There is a problem facing the country. Well, maybe they were not good managers. Maybe they did not work hard enough. Mr. Speaker, I say to you that the small-business men with whom I am acquainted all put in a tremendous amount of effort, time and work in order to make their businesses go. You have to be impressed with the long hours those individuals spend in their businesses to try to make them successful. It might be a small corner grocery store employing four or five people, or it might be a small restaurant employing five or ten people. All of these operations contribute more to the over-all economy of the country than one of the large businesses that we hear is in the midst of a downturn and is laying off personnel. These small businesses are the ones that provide the jobs necessary for our young people to learn what it is like to work when they first start out working after school and on Saturdays. This also applies to the young lady and young man who leave school to go to work. Yet we are not alarmed at the present state of affairs. In 1981 a record 8,055 businesses were forced to close their doors forever. Business bankcruptcies were 22 per cent more numerous than in 1980, and 43 per cent more numerous than in 1979. These are alarming figures.
What do we do to assist the small-business man? What can we do to tell him that we really appreciate his having taken a gamble, putting his investment money into a business and employing five, six or seven people. We really reward the small entrepreneur. How do we do that? The Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) brings in a budget that attacks the small remuneration or the perks, if you will, that a small-business man gets. For example, the small-business man, because of this budget, can no longer buy a car in the company name. He
Small Businesses Loans Act (No. 3)
cannot put it in the name of this little grocery store, his restaurant or his hardware store because that car is now considered part of his wages. The government does not consider that a man or a woman may have to work 16 or 18 hours a day to make his business operation viable. The government does not stop to consider a team of a husband and wife who work 16 and 18 hours a day and employ three or more other people who have to remit to the government the necessary unemployment insurance deductions, the necessary pension deductions and the necessary income tax deductions. Small business people are collecting tax. They become collectors. But no, the government does not consider that. It does not consider that a businessman is now paying himself the minimum wage in order to survive because he has to pour everything back into his business. Instead, the government thinks that the small-business man might be getting away with driving a pickup truck, that he might use it to get his own mail or he might use it on a Sunday to take his wife and family on a little picnic. Because the businessman is doing that, the government has to watch what he does. The government considers that the businessman and the farmer are ripping off the country by having a tax loophole. The government fails to remember that the small-business man is drawing the minimum wage for himself and his family, on which the government taxes him. The pickup truck becomes imputed, and it is as though it is received as income. That is how we reward the initiative of the individual coming out of school who said that he wants to be independent, go into business and build something for himself. That is what this country was made of. This country was made by those who did not want to work for somebody else but who wanted to get out and do it for themselves.
The same could be said of the farmers. There are many young lads who say, "That is for me. I want to be productive. I want to grow food for the nation and for the world." But what do we do for them? We should bring in a bill that addresses the cost of fuel and fertilizer and recognizes the fact that if these people do not produce, we do not eat. The cost of farm fuels is creeping up to where it takes 40 per cent to 45 per cent of all productions costs. Do hon. members know that 40 per cent to 45 per cent of all farming costs are fuel related, either in tractor fuel, fertilizer, or pesticides? And we wonder why farmers are going bankrupt.
Let us take a look at and put some more statistics on the record. Let us go back to 1981. A record 8,055 businesses went bankrupt and closed their doors forever. That includes farms. In 1982, in the first five months alone there were 4,429 bankruptcies. Already in the first five months, there have been over half as many as for the whole of 1981. That is an increase of 36 per cent over the first five months of 1981. It is an increase of 55 per cent over the first five months of 1980. Those figures are alarming when we consider that over 55 per cent of all the jobs from Prince Edward Island to Vancouver Island to the Northwest Territories and the Yukon are created by small-business men. These are not rich businessmen but small, little fellows.

July 23, 1982
Small Businesses Loans Act (No. 3)
We are bringing in a bill that will help 5,000 businessmen because we are extending a loan guarantee that is controlled by the bank. The banks says they can give a loan of one per cent above prime on $100,000. The government will guarantee it. Five thousand businessmen will be helped. But that does not help them. They still have to pay above prime for the money they have to borrow, and they will float their inventory.
Why are we not bringing in legislation to extend the Small Business Development Bond which was introduced by the Conservative government, which is now reluctantly being carried forward by the present government to assist businesses going bankrupt? Why is the government not considering extending the Small Business Development Bond to an extent that would allow the small-business man to borrow at half prime plus one or two per cent? This was a tax measure, and all it did was to disallow the small-business man from claiming interest as an expense on his operation. Because the bank was lending money at half prime plus one or two per cent, depending upon the bank, that was brought in as a dividend from the small business and it was taxed at a different rate from that of the bank. We all know the problems the banks are facing today.
Surely it makes no difference to the government if this small business development bond is used for healthy and viable growth of a company. Why is it being used only for businesses on the verge of bankruptcy or with severe financial difficulties? What businessman would want to walk into a bank and say, "I would like a Small Business Development Bond application; I want to apply because I am having serious financial difficulties"? This is not what they want to do. We should have legislation before the House which makes the Small Business Development Bond available to healthy and viable companies, not a piece of legislation which means absolutely nothing. It would be an extension of a program which has been in operation for years and affects at the most 5,000 businesses across the country at any one time. Actually, in Toronto alone there would be 5,000 businesses. I just do not understand.
Mr. Bergen Mr. Speaker, 1 rise on a point of order. I know the hon. member would not want to mislead the Canadian public. He referred to a figure of 5,000 businesses which had benefited from the program in the past year. The number of loans approved during the past year was 16,942. It was substantially more than 5,000.
