In the first five months of 1981 there were 183, and in the first five months of 1982 there were 266. It seems to me that in the primary sector, which includes farming and food production, there is a crisis approaching that is not being addressed. We have heard talk about an energy crisis, a currency crisis and so on, but if we lose the primary sector, we do not eat. We cannot eat oil.
Now let me turn to the statistics in terms of small business bankruptcies in the manufacturing sector. In the first five months of 1980, 239 businesses went bankrupt. In the first five months of 1981, there were 240, only one more, and in 1982 they almost doubled to 418. These statistics are alarming.
In the construction industry, 586 small businesses went bankrupt in the first five months of 1980. In the first five months of 1981, they went down by one to 585, and in the first five months of 1982, there were 685 bankruptcies. I hope hon. members find these statistics alarming.
In the first five months of 1980, 195 small businesses in transportation, communications and utilities went bankrupt. In the first five months of 1981, 202 went bankrupt, and in the first five months of 1982 there were 305 small business bankruptcies. As I say, I find these statistics alarming. We are not addressing this problem in the House. Certainly it is not being addressed by the government in Bill C-122, to extend a program which affects 16,000 businesses across the country. It will not do anything for them.
Let me turn to small businesses connected with trade. In the first five months of 1980, 970 businesses went bankrupt; in the first five months of 1981, 1,059 went bankrupt; in the first five months of 1982, 1,374 went bankrupt. The graph is going up and up. What will happen when I stand here next year to talk about the first five months of 1983? We are in serious trouble.
If hon. members opposite accept the proposition that small businesses provide 55 per cent of all jobs across Canada, then they must accept the proposition that we are in serious difficulty. The government is not doing anything to assist small-business men to keep them viable and to keep over 50 per cent
July 23, 1982

of the work force employed. This is to our peril. I do not care what the government wants to do, but it cannot create a Crown corporation like Petro-Canada to look after all shoe repair shops, all groceries stores, all barber shops and all other small businesses in the country. We must keep small-business men healthy and viable. If we do not have a healthy business community within the community as a whole, we do not have a healthy country. Small-business men are the ones to whom the service clubs go. They are the ones who coach minor league hockey teams or peewee ball teams. Hon. members opposite should go out there to see who sponsors such teams. In essence, small-business men determine whether or not we have a healthy Canada.
I would like to turn to small businesses in finance, insurance and real estate. In the first five months of 1980, 107 small businesses in finance, insurance and real estate went bankrupt. In the first five months of 1981, 103 of these small businesses went bankrupt. In the first five months of 1982, 197 small businesses went bankrupt. I guarantee to all hon. members that in the first five months of 1983 in the finance, insurance and real estate field they will see that figure of 197 go up as high as 500.
It is a reflection of what is happening in our economy. The real estate and insurance markets are dropping because people are not buying homes. Nor will they be buying homes with the $3,000 grant such as the one the minister presented to someone in Edmonton. It is baffling how they picked that individual because the forms for the home owner grants are not available in any of the offices. The minister must have picked him out of the blue.
In the service industry there were 646 businesses that went bankrupt in the first five months of 1980. He said: Mr. Speaker, the time taken away from the private members' hour this afternoon does not really cause me much concern. I will be quite brief.
Because of a problem in my personal timing, this bill is delayed in coming before the House more than it perhaps might have been. I would have preferred to have had this bill brought forward some months ago prior to a bill of a similar nature, Bill C-223, in the name of my friend and colleague for Red Deer (Mr. Towers). However, as I said, it was a timing problem on my part that held it up. As a consequence, 1 will be very brief.
The subject matter of this bill has been before the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections. 1 would have hoped that even at this late date I might convince the deputy to the House leader that this subject matter might still go the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections.
The basic contention of the bill is that there is absolutely no reason for increasing the number of members in this House of
Representation Act, 1980
Commons. I am going to take a moment to read into the record part of the explanation for my bill that will give some background and substantiation for that statement.
I want to point out particularly that in the bill which I mentioned a moment ago in the name of my colleague for Red Deer there is one similarity. We have both asked that the basic benchmark for determining the number of members in the House of Commons that was set some years ago, 75 members of the Province of Quebec, to be increased by four at each subsequent decennial census, not be decreased but held at 75.
The step I have taken beyond that, which is slightly different, is that the 1981 census be ignored in its entirety. Hon. members will know that the results of the 1971 census were not brought into being until 1979 so that the boundaries were not changed until eight years after the census was taken. Given the timing of the census and the timing of the next election, it is possible that new boundaries could be struck prior to the next election. That would have meant there would have been one extremely short Parliament and one long Parliament with these boundaries we now have.
1 refer briefly to an excellent column which appeared this week written by Douglas Fisher, the well-known columnist and some time ago member of the New Democratic Party who sat in this House. He points out the relevance of the possible date of the next election and that the redistribution process cannot be completed before December 1984. That is the redistribution process that would follow from the 1981 census.
We would expect that the next election will likely be held in 1984, given the last election in 1980 and the tradition of having elections approximately every four years. However, we need only go back two elections to realize that the Parliament elected in 1974 lasted until 1979. If this Parliament were to sit that long, we could be faced with a redistribution prior to the next election. That is totally unnecessary.
If that were to happen, we would be faced with the accomplished fact of an increase in the number of members in this House. I do not see that. In his speech on his private members' bill and during his appearances before the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections, my colleague from Red Deer made a number of arguments for holding the House at the present figure or perhaps allowing it to increase by eight or ten seats.
I know that my friend opposite, the hon. member for Mississauga North (Mr. Fisher) will speak following me. I am sure he will put on record, as will my colleague from the Brampton area, the fact that they represent ridings that extend far and beyond the 25 per cent over the base that is allowed. They represent ridings that are double the population and more close to the norm that was set as a result of the 1971 census and the procedure that is followed. I hope that my colleague from Mississauga North will tell the House that while handling a constituency of that size is extremely difficult, if given the tools and the staff he would not have a great deal of difficulty.

After all, our colleagues in the United States House of Representatives handle in the order of 400,000 constituents. However, if my cause had any justification to it at all, I had absolutely no difficulty in putting my point across.
One of the arguments made by Mr. Fisher, or alluded to-I should not say it is an argument made by him because he does not put a lot of weight behind it-is that because there are only 75,000 people in my constituency, and the constituency of my friend, the hon. member for Mississauga North, has over
150,000,	his votes carry only half the weight of mine. I disagree with that argument. Frankly, it seems to me that if my colleague across the way can make his point and get his arguments through the House of Commons, his people are equally well represented, and there is no less weight behind the votes his constituents cast than behind the votes cast by people in the less-populated Prince Edward-Hastings constituency.
I argue very strenuously that this House should not be enlarged. I would not have a problem if the House were enlarged by eight or ten seats. If the evidence given before the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections this year by the deputy to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Pinard) is accurate, then by freezing the representation of Quebec at 75 seats, the House would increase in size by eight or ten seats.
I do see that as a problem, but if the size of the House were to grow any larger than that, I feel that would be quite unnecessary.
Surprisingly, this matter has been the subject of letters to the editor in the city of Belleville. It is not a subject matter I
thought would have caught the attention of very many people, yet Mr. Sidney Sillitoe, who was a friend for many years, without any discussion with me but, rather, in discussions with others in the city of Belleville, realized that the House would be enlarged because of the decennial census. In letters to the editor people were complaining that this should not happen. So it is that a subject which we would normally have thought would have occupied the minds only of those people within the House of Commons to varying degrees is one which has caught the interest of people within my constituency. If it is there, I am sure it is also in other places.
I want to close by saying once again that I can see absolutely no justification for having the size of this House increased, and I strongly urge members of the government opposite to refer the subject matter of this particular bill to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections to allow the committee to deal with it, albeit much later this year.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: REPRESENTATION ACT, 1980 MEASURE TO STABILIZE REPRESENTATION IN HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I extend my thanks to my colleague, the hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings (Mr. Ellis), for giving me an opportunity to talk about a very important issue to me personally. I am rising now not to make an official speech but to give my personal opinion based on my own experiences in Mississauga North.
I represent the second most populated riding in Canada. The most populated one, York-Scarborough, is held by a minister, so I suppose I hold the record as an ordinary member.
In 1980, there were 93,000 voters registered in my riding. That is the firmest evidence I have of its size. They were registered voters and, of course, on top of that there are all the children, all the non-citizens and all the people who were missed on the list. The estimate in the newspaper the other day indicated that there are approximately 190,000 people in my
July 23, 1982

riding. On top of that, just to let hon. members know some more details, my constituency is an area of very rapid population expansion. Recently, the city of Mississauga approved three new subdivisions, which will bring a total of 25,000 new homes into my area. Those homes will be added before we have an opportunity to redistribute the riding. Assuming that there will be two or three people living in each of them, I will have a gigantic riding by the time redistribution gets around to me.
I do not care whether we add more members to this House of Commons or whether we do some kind of shuffling, but certainly people in my area are mistreated by this system, and I hope to put that argument forward and to prove my case. It is that opportunity I appreciate today.
There are three electoral problems facing my riding. The first is that the general political workload involved is very, very heavy. I personally have no problem with that. In fact, the opportunities to go to spring festivals, parades, community centres and all sorts of community events help me to break down the anonymity of my riding. The political work is my work. I chose Mississauga to run in, and I am happy to represent the area. I am delighted all that work is there.
There are two radio stations, a very effective cable television station and four neighbourhood newspapers, all of which help me to break down the size of my constituency. We have ongoing neighbourhood and volunteer groups which help me to become known to people and to work on their problems. The political work is my responsibility, but I remind hon. members that on other occasions and in other precedents the workload facing hon. members has been considered a reasonable justification for giving members additional resources. I will come back to that point.
The second problem facing the people in my area is that their individual problems are difficult to communicate to their Member of Parliament. Because my area contains so many people and because of its size it is hard for the people to get in touch with me. When the people do get in touch with me, they have a difficult time making their cases, simply because of the workload. I do not know what happens in the offices of other hon. members, but my office has kept track and has found that in busy periods during the winter it is very common for us to receive 50 telephone calls a day dealing with personal problems. When people telephone me and say, "Doug, you are doing a lousy job", I feel that is an opinion, so I do not include that in that count. However, people telephone me and say, "Doug, I want to get my grandmother into the country. She lives in India and is having a difficult time because of our demands with respect to immigration." That is a problem which requires a great deal of work in order to serve the constituent properly. I take that very personally. I do not think that is a partisan issue. I do not think that is an opinion. That is an obligation on me as a Member of Parliament, and I cannot always carry out my responsibilities fully, simply because of the demands that are made. In my office I maintain two full-time people. We have three telephone lines coming in. Another person works half the week in my office. All of this is paid for out of the budget of the House of Commons, although
Representation Act, 1980
my riding association makes a contribution because the House of Commons budget cannot cover it all. We keep the office open from nine o'clock until five o'clock every day and there is a telephone answering machine for the evenings and the weekend.
Because we are talking about large ridings we should realize the cost involved. One cannot hope to keep up the work with the resources now available, which are based on the experience of smaller areas.
Finally, we have the important question of representing the voice of our people in government. According to the chief returning officer, the average riding had about 55,000 registered voters in the last election. My riding had 93,000 people. They have a diluted voice in Ottawa, and I am sorry about that. But the one-man one-vote principle has been tested over and over again and is diluted in these circumstances. We heard that effectiveness and hard work by the MP would offset this imbalance. The hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings made that point, and of course he is right. A good, strong, clear voice will carry a long way. But he overlooked the fact that in politics ultimately it is numbers that count. Two votes are more than one, and in politics the number of votes decides issues. That is an important principle, which is being diluted by the fact that my riding has one member for 93,000 voters while the average riding has one member for 55,000 voters. That represents a dilution of impact in my area.
We have acknowledged the one-man one-vote principle in our processes and we try to come as close as we can to it. The decade-long cycle is too cumbersome and too slow, however. In trying to be absolutely fair and prevent abuse, we create unfairness through delay. I think the ratios could be corrected in one way or another if we acted more quickly.
Let me give an example of this, Mr. Speaker. There was a general census in 1971 which led to the decision on redistributing the electoral boundaries in 1975. Those new boundaries were to come into effect in the next general election. As we all know, however, in 1978 in York-Scarborough a byelection was fought on the basis of the old boundaries. Today, that same area is represented by three Members of Parliament. The process is too slow and cumbersome, Mr. Speaker. In 1978 the voters from what is today Don Valley East, York Centre and York Scarborough all voted in that one byelection.
In 1971, Mississauga was one riding. It was fought and won by my Liberal predecessor, the hon. Tony Abbott in 1974. In 1979 it was split in two, and in 1980 when I fought the election the area was big enough for three ridings. Yet 1979 and 1980 is when the new boundaries came into effect. There is too great a gap between the census and the enactment of the new boundaries, Mr. Speaker. I am concerned that this cycle will be repeated over and over again.
We have had the 1981 census, and the estimates are that it will be 1985 before the new boundaries are applicable. If the normal electoral cycle is followed, that means that the new

July 23, 1982
Representation Act, 1980
boundaries will not come into effect until the late 1980s. My area will probably have three ridings and, according to the normal projection, by the late 1980s the population will be big enough to call for four ridings.
I have some suggestions to offer to help deal with this situation, and they are concentrated mainly on the problem of representation on behalf of the ordinary citizen living in a big area like mine. I believe we should recognize the principle that one-man one-vote is not enough. We should also recognize that people make work for politicians. We should put in place a separate category or riding-the big riding, where growth and size are very important.
There is already a geographical precedent. It has been recognized that the hon. member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson) has special problems and special work because of the vast area he represents. He has been given some extra resources to help him out. I think that is necessary because the geography creates extra work in his case. But people make work in politics too, Mr. Speaker. There are 190,000 people in my riding, each of whom deserves my full attention. Therefore, I should have extra resources as well.
I should like to issue a challenge to the hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings. He is a member of the Standing Committee on Management and Members' Services. That committee deals with problems like this. A year ago I wrote to that committee and proposed that extra resources be allocated to people representing huge and expanding ridings. I presented a petition signed by ten Liberal members and I asked that two NDP members and about ten Conservative members also make representations. I was told by the hon. member for Brampton-Georgetown (Mr. McDermid) that those representations were going forward from the Conservatives, and I was told by the hon. member for Comox-Powell River (Mr. Skelly) that representations were going forward on behalf of his party. They landed in the hands of the hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings and a few others and disappeared in a vacuum. I must say that I think it is about time that we had a report on the situation from the committee.
We suggested a very simple procedure, that the regular redistribution be supplemented with extra resources after each election. When enumeration takes place and voters lists are produced, a national average of riding size should be established based on the number of voters rather than on population. Ridings in the top ten per cent size should be allocated money to enable the MP to employ an extra staff person to deal with the burdens of the representation of the larger number of people in those ridings. Unfortunately, nothing has been heard from the committee. I would urge its members, especially the hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings whose conscience on this issue is so clear, to give an answer to this proposal soon. I would ask the hon. member to acknowledge at least that people make work and that huge ridings have special demands.
I would be prepared to debate, somewhere else, in philosophical terms, the second question of whether the people in my riding have a diluted voice because they have only one member
for so many voters, and so on. It is an important issue which needs to be discussed. I think we all agree that the redistribution procedure, whether it adds extra people or makes a change in the boundaries, could be speeded up.
The third area where 1 indicated there was a problem was in the area of political representation. I think the cure for political problems and political representation is to encourage the good people of Mississauga North, numerous as they are, to keep on voting Liberal.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 intend to be very brief in addressing the bill before us. I would like to say I share the sentiments of the hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings (Mr. Ellis), if we continue to grow like Topsy. This is what will happen if we do not make some adjustments to the current set-up which would see this House with something like 300, or in excess of 300 members in the next redistribution. I am in somewhat the same position as the hon. member in discussing this, and that reminds me of something which Peter Ustinov said a few years ago. 1 find myself of two minds on the subject, one more or less in disagreement with the other.
I come from a constituency called Kootenay West which currently has the smallest population of any constituency in British Columbia. It has 500 people less than any other riding in the province. I have 58,000 population, to be exact. If we were to alter the formula in the way envisaged in this bill, we would likely have to add additional population to the riding, and to many other rural or urban ridings than is presently the case, or would be, based on present census figures and the redistribution that will come as a result of it. Under the current regime the riding will have 11,000 less than the next smallest riding, although it will still come above the 25 per cent variable which applies to most constituencies across Canada.
While I appreciate the remarks of the hon. member opposite who has just spoken, it may be that we will have to give increasing consideration over the long haul to servicing those constituencies with significantly larger populations, complicated as that is because of the time lag on the census and redistribution. But we also have to bear in mind the rather unique problems that are faced, and which have been recognized in the past by those of us in rural and rural urban ridings.
My own riding encompases some 13 municipalities. One of my colleagues from Saskatchewan has a combination of 80 Indian bands and municipalities within one constituency. Those kinds of burdens also place additional responsibilities on the members who represent those areas. They are in a sense mini-republics and the consultative mechanisms that have to be put in place in order to keep a semblance of orderly communication between a member and all the component organized parts of his constituency require some additional effort, both quantitatively and quality-wise than I suspect is the case in many urban constituencies. While they may have large
July 23, 1982

numbers of people they are more homogeneous and of one mind on particular subject matters and areas.
Having said all that, I do agree with the hon. member who introduced the bill that the nightmare we can envision happening in this chamber, both physically and how it will affect other workings, is and will be getting worse and worse on the basis of the current formula. I do not think any one of us has the magic answer. It would seem to me that if we do put the kind of formula in place which the hon. member is suggesting, then we must also reconsider the variable formula and 25 per cent variance which is currently allowed as between populations of our various constituencies.
Another matter that needs to be looked at by the committee is further refinement of the redistribution process, even once the formula has been worked out. In the last redistribution within my own area, even though the process we now have is a significant improvement over the mechanism that used to take place a number of years ago in terms of sorting out constituency boundaries, I know of one situation where a community of eight people, the poll of Trout Lake, which has a long continuing historical connection with the remainder of my constituency, was suddenly put into the constituency of Kootenay East-Revelstoke. Kootenay East-Revelstoke is some 100 miles away over gravel and dirt roads. That single poll of only eight people, who could otherwise communicate back and forth with the remainder of the constituency over a distance of 30 miles, are now forced to go 100 miles in order to have anything in common at all with the constituency with which they are a part. Their only established link is that traditionally they have been serviced by the Revelstoke Post Office. This is like a Len Norris cartoon of earlier Vancouver Sun fame; the little old lady who used to cover her eyes and stick a pin in a ballot. I suspect that is the only way that kind of arbitrary decision could have been made in terms of sorting out those boundaries.
We are also left with the situation that there are two time zones within the constituency. The riding is established in this way to take in 500 people who would fit much better into the adjoining constituency. Those anomalies would not be corrected by this bill. In any continuing discussion of redistribution, I think we should be looking at that process and trying to define it a little more delicately.
Basically, I support the intent of the bill before us, as do most of my colleagues. Our overriding concern is that this House should continue to be of a size that is at least somewhat workable, both in terms of quantity and quality, so that we can do the kind of job that is expected of us by all our constituents.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to thank hon. members for their courtesy. 1 certainly support my colleague, the hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings (Mr. Ellis). I have sympathy for the hon. member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn). Years ago I had the most populated riding west of Scarborough, and I got along quite well. True enough, the demands upon the member at that time were not as great.
I think the solution lies partly in what the hon. member is advocating. I do not think the suggestion that every member should be entitled to the same number of staff and so forth is right. It seems to me that the facilities for a member should be geared to a mathematical formula based upon the size of his riding.
There is one thing which the hon. member for Mississauga South fails to realize, and that is that we do have flaws here. Prince Edward Island has four members. The total population of the province is barely over 120,000. There is the same difficulty in New Brunswick, Newfoundland, Nova Scotia and Saskatchewan. You are not going to get away from disparate numbers in any way. It seems to me that the solution lies in according facilities to a member based upon the population of his constituency.
There is one final point I should like to make. The chamber should have no more than 240 members. There has been an improvement in communications and in facilities compared with what they were when I first came to the House 25 years ago. In fact, they are incomparable. With appropriate staffing facilities, members can look after greater populations. There is no way that the Chamber can accommodate any more members in a practical sense. There is already overpressure on question period, on debating time and in committees. We must resort to silly nonsense, to the point that a member now has five minutes to question witnesses in the committee consideration of Bill C-124. If a witness takes 3.5 minutes to answer, then the time is gone.
We should reduce the number of our committees. We could handle things much better. At the present time the chamber is growing like Topsy, and I must say that the pis-aller solution which was found in the mid-1970s to deal with a totally bad system of redistribution built a Frankenstein into the system.
The contents of this bill should go to committee. I do not think there should be total discouragement of this proposal. I hope hon. members on the government side will agree that the contents of my colleague's bill should go to the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization.

Representation Act, 1980
The problems of the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Kristiansen) and those who represent coastal constituencies are matters of redistribution. The people at fault are the redistribution commissioners. It is not a question of the number of seats.
Therefore I support this bill. I urge hon. members not to talk it out, but to let its contents go to the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization so there will be a full exchange of ideas. This would benefit all members of the House. We have done that time immemorial. These proposals should not be talked out. They should be discussed in greater detail in a committee designed to look after the problems of the House.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, although it is a beautiful day outside, we are always pleased to take part in the Friday afternoon debate, and 1 am particularly interested in this one because the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings (Mr. Ellis) would impose a certain restriction on the province of Quebec. The hon. member claims that Bill C-276 is designed to stabilize the representation in the House. I would like to read the act as it is now and then compare it with the amendment of the hon. member. Section 51 of the British North America Act reads as follows, and I quote:
"51. (1) The number of members of the House of Commons and the representation of the provinces therein shall upon the coming into force of this subsection and thereafter on the completion of each decennial census be readjusted by such authority, in such manner, and from such time as the Parliament of Canada from time to time provides, subject and according to the following Rules:
1. There shall be assigned to Quebec seventy-five members in the readjustment following the completion of the decennial census taken in the year 1971, and thereafter four additional members in each subsequent readjustment."
Now here is the amendment of the hon. member:
All that portion of subsection 51(1) of the British North America Act, 1867, as enacted by the British North America Act, 1974, that precedes Rule 1 thereof is repealed and the following substituted therefor:
"51. (1) The number of members of the House of Commons and the representation of the provinces therein shall upon the completion of each decennial census, commencing with the census taken in the year 1991, be readjusted by the authority, in the manner, and at the time provided by the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act, subject and according to the following Rules respecting the relative representation of the provinces:"
He then goes on to say:
Rule 1 of the said subsection is repealed and the following substituted therefor: "1. There shall be assigned to Quebec seventy-five members in each readjustment."
And the words:
-four additional members in each subsequent readjustment-
-are completely omitted.
Mr. Speaker, it would be useful at this stage for me to go back to the time when I was a teacher as well as a notary and that I provide some background in an attempt to explain how the act and the electoral boundaries readjustment process now work. There is a brochure published by the Chief Electoral Officer entitled "Representation in the Federal Parliament" that is available to the public and Canadians would be well advised to write either to their own Member of Parliament or to any other member to obtain this very interesting publication. If I may, I would like this afternoon to tell Canadians what has happened since 1867. I am sure that many people have unfortunately no idea of what has happened. This publication says the following:
Canada owes its legislative body to the British North America Act of 1867. The Upper House, or Senate, was to include 24 members and this representation was to remain the same regardless of shifts in population. On the other hand, the number of members of the House of Commons was determined according to the principle of representation by population. This institution was to have included, "subject to the provisions of this act", 181 members: 82 for Ontario, 65 for Quebec, 19 for Nova Scotia and 15 for New Brunswick. Section 51 of the BN A Act stated that the seats in the House should be redistributed among the provinces after the 1871 census. This redistribution was to follow each decennial census, "by such authority, in such manner, and from such time, as the Parliament of Canada from time to time provides". The readjustment rules provided under the act set at 65 the number of seats assigned to Quebec, and the representation of the other provinces was to increase or decrease according to the relative number of their population. The only exception to this form of proportional representation was the one-twentieth rule under which no province could lose seats following redistribution unless the percentage of the total population of the country represented by its own population had decreased by at least 5 per cent during the period between the latest census and the previous one.
The original rules applied from 1871 to 1946, or more than 75 years. The only change made during this period consisted in adding in 1915 the "Senate rule" which provides that a province cannot have fewer seats in the House of Commons than in the Senate.
Mr. Speaker, before 1946, no maximum limit was set for the number of seats in the House of Commons. I notice that my time is nearly up, but I would like to close by saying that, in my opinion, maintaining the status quo or the formula provided in the act represents the protection which I believe we need in Quebec. I must say that if there had been a vote, 1 would have kept to this position and voted against the bill of the hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings (Mr. Ellis) in spite of his good intentions. It still remains that maintaining the status quo is the best position that a Quebec member can take.
